That's not what "selfish gene" means. A "selfish gene" is a metaphor about how genes act in ways to preserve themselves(hence, the selfish part.) In actuality, a "selfish gene" can cause us to act in ways that are nearly the opposite of what we commonly perceive as "selfish." For example, a "selfish gene" could cause us to risk our lives to save the lives of others either for increased prestige, or to defend our genes in others or, (insert your own theory here.) I think the author is "weak-man"ing the human nature argument here. I do not human-beings were built as egalitarians. I think it's human nature to prioritize certain lives (including our own) above others. For example, if your (hypothetical child) was in a burning building with a lot of children, and you only had time to save one kid, who do you think you would be most likely to save? That's an extreme example, but it's to make a point. Certain traits are in-born in the vast majority of human beings, and I doubt they'll be conditioned out anytime soon. A well-functioning society will create mechanisms to use these in-born traits in ways that everyone gains from them. Markets do this rather well. Markets use selfishness to increase our incentives to cooperate and to produce resources for others.
